stages.title: AI can talk. It cannot reach your tools
stages.desc: A model answers from memory. It has no native route into GitHub, your database, your files or Slack.

stages.title: Every tool speaks a different language
stages.desc: Seven tools, seven APIs, seven bespoke integrations — and every AI app has to build all of them again.

stages.title: One protocol replaces all of them
stages.desc: MCP is a single open standard for how an AI app asks any tool for data, and how that tool answers.

stages.title: Client on your side, server on the tool's
stages.desc: The AI app runs an MCP client. Each tool is wrapped by an MCP server. Requests go down, results come back up.

stages.title: Watch a single request travel
stages.desc: Read my GitHub repository — the ask goes down the stack, and the repo data comes back up as an answer.

stages.title: One prompt, many tools
stages.desc: Read today’s sales from SQL and post a summary to Slack — the model chains two MCP servers on its own.

stages.title: Build once, connect everywhere
stages.desc: One MCP server per tool, reused by every AI app you ever ship. M + N connectors instead of M × N.

stages.title: One protocol. Unlimited integrations
stages.desc: User, assistant, MCP client, MCP server, and every tool you already run — all on one open standard.

end.title: MCP is the port every AI tool plugs into
end.sub: One open protocol between your assistant and GitHub, SQL, files, Slack, the browser, your calendar and Azure — write the connector once, reuse it everywhere.

post.caption:
A model that cannot reach your systems is a very expensive autocomplete.

Before MCP, every AI app rebuilt every integration by hand: GitHub over REST and OAuth, SQL over ODBC, Slack over its Web API, the browser over CDP. Seven apps and seven tools means forty-nine integrations, all of them someone’s problem forever.

The Model Context Protocol collapses that. The AI app runs an MCP client, each tool is wrapped by an MCP server, and both sides speak one standard covering tools, resources and prompts. Seven connectors instead of forty-nine — and the model can chain them, pulling today’s sales out of SQL and posting the summary to Slack from a single prompt.

M + N instead of M × N. That is the whole idea.
